chapter: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
title: RCA-NBC broadcast recordings and Decca versus RCA sound
summary: Welburn lists Webb's January 1939 RCA radio sides; McRae returns to his complaint about Decca's sound and Milt Gabler.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: I see in the Rust Discography there's an NBC broadcast from the Blue Room of the Hotel Lincoln in New York.
There are just two selections here. There's One O'Clock Jump and The Blue Room.
That's available on Polydor. I believe that's a -- that's probably a French release.
There's also a series of French -- of Polydors for RCA Victor -- recorded by RCA Victor for NBC.

This was in January of 1939. There are several selections there. 'Liza', All The Crowds Are All Away, 'Who Ya Hunchin', 'Dinah', 'Blue Skies', 'Bye Heck', 'Grand Terrace Rhythm', 'Sugar Foot Stomp', 'Crazy
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Rhythm, 'Blue Room,' 'One O'Clock Jump,' (inaudible), 'Tea For Two.'

I think those are the things that Chick did -- Remember I was telling you that I had did -- Those were the dates that we did at the RCA. You remember I was criticizing Decca --when I went back to Decca --

For the sound quality. We weren't getting the sound quality (inaudible). Remember I told you Erskine Hawkins had made that Tuxedo Junction and his band sound so better than our band, you know. In sound-wise, you know. It's in sound-wise. Remember that 'Tuxedo Junction' was a big hit? And it had a good quality. RCA was turning out much better quality. And we would go into Decca, we would come out -- we couldn't hear the background of the instruments. We used to play this bass clarinets

delicate (inaudible) stuff behind it -- all the flutes and stuff. That was all buried like. It was buried like. You could hardly hear that stuff. So it was an argument going on between -- in Decca. Dave Cavanaugh -- not Dave Cavanaugh, the other fellow, Milt Gabler, you know. He says, "Hey, we're doing all right. You know, the records are selling." But I wanted a better sound out of the records that we were doing, because these things at RCA Victor, they sound great. Remember I told you they had great rooms down there?
Because I remember being down there with Fats Waller, (inaudible) my brothers recorded down there. Their things were coming out good, real good.
